title: Which expressions describe the two statements?
description: Two statements in words are turned into expressions with a letter: two more than a square number, and the sum of the squares of two numbers that follow each other. Each option is tested by putting in a number, as the pattern expressions were.
teaching_notes: One idea: write the statement with a letter, then test every option with a number. Watch for students who pick the square of s plus two for two more than a square.

source: Figure it Out (identities and patterns, question 3)
video_script.why: The child has written an expression for a pattern and tested it with a step number, and now picks expressions for statements in words in the same way.
video_script.substitution: Write the statement with a letter, put in a number such as three, and keep only the options that give the same value.
video_script.anchor: the two statements with their lists of expressions on option cards
video_script.payoff_line: Two more than a square number is s squared plus two

final_answer.spoken: part one is s squared plus two; part two is m squared plus the square of m plus one, and m squared plus the square of m minus one

maths_rules: (i) a square number is s²; two more than it is s² + 2
s = 3: square number 9, two more is 11; s² + 2 = 11; (s + 2)² = 25; s² + 4 = 13; 2s² = 18; 2²s = 12; 2 + s = 5; only s² + 2 gives 11
(ii) two numbers one after the other are m and m + 1, or m − 1 and m; sums of squares m² + (m + 1)² and m² + (m − 1)²
m = 3: m² + 1 = 10; (m + (m + 1))² = 7² = 49; (2m)² + (2m + 1)² = 36 + 49 = 85 = 6² + 7², the squares of 6 and 7, so it fits only pairs whose smaller number is even
m² + n² has no link between m and n
video_script.design: One idea: write the statement with a letter, then test each option with a number. The two statements stay in the anchor band; each test sits on the working board.
open_questions: In part (i), 2 + s also fits if s itself is the square number; the worklist takes s as the number being squared, so only s² + 2 is kept.
In part (ii), (2m)² + (2m + 1)² is the sum of squares of two numbers that follow each other when the smaller is even; the worklist keeps only the two expressions that fit every pair.

narration: <bookmark mark='letter'/>First, take statement one. Let the number be s.
<bookmark mark='square'/>The square number is s squared.
<bookmark mark='more'/>Two more than it is s squared plus two.

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Second, test the options with s as three. The square number is nine, and two more is eleven.
<bookmark mark='fit'/>The expression s squared plus two gives eleven, so it fits.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>The square of s plus two is twenty five. S squared plus four is thirteen, and two s squared is eighteen.
<bookmark mark='last'/>Two squared times s is twelve, and two plus s is five. None of these is eleven.

beats.on_screen: (ii) m, m + 1: m² + (m + 1)²; m − 1, m: m² + (m − 1)²

marks.pair: the numbers m and m + 1 are written
marks.other: the pair m − 1 and m and m² + (m − 1)² are written

narration: <bookmark mark='pair'/>Third, take statement two. Two numbers, one after the other, are m and m plus one.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>The sum of their squares is m squared plus the square of m plus one.
<bookmark mark='other'/>The pair could also be m minus one and m. Then the sum is m squared plus the square of m minus one.

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Fourth, test the other options with m as three, for the numbers three and four.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>M squared plus one is ten. The square of m plus m plus one is forty nine.
<bookmark mark='big'/>The option built from two m gives eighty five, the squares of six and seven. It fits only pairs whose smaller number is even.
<bookmark mark='two'/>M squared plus n squared has no link between m and n, so it fits nothing.

marks.plus: m = 3 gives m² + (m + 1)² = 9 + 16 = 25 and is ticked
marks.minus: m = 4 gives m² + (m − 1)² = 16 + 9 = 25 and is ticked

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Fifth, put the answers back in the question. The squares of three and four add to nine plus sixteen, which is twenty five.
<bookmark mark='plus'/>With m as three, the first sum is nine plus sixteen, twenty five.
<bookmark mark='minus'/>With m as four, the second sum is sixteen plus nine, twenty five again.
